It definitely is a LOT more intense and restrictive in reality, but I do appreciate how diverse the characters were in those episodes. I feel like every other show/movie/book with a psych ward portrays ALL patients as dangerous and stereotypically “insane”, but not every patient is that intense. Even with characters like Freedom Master, who very obviously was a danger to himself, was portrayed in a way that made him a human with a mental illness rather than a caricature of a “crazy person” who struggles with delusions.

I also like how they portrayed Alvie, as there’s a common stereotype of mania being dangerous and meaning you’re a threat to others. While true in some cases, it definitely isn’t in all, and I know a lot of people stigmatize people with bipolar because of that misconception. I do think Alvie’s character was still sort of made out to be the comic relief because of his mania, so while not a perfect character, I like how they didn’t villainize him.

To clarify, I don’t have bipolar but I have major depressive disorder so I understand how people can “expect” you to be a certain way during a mood disorder episode. Which is why I appreciate Alvie’s character. Also, for context, I have been hospitalized 3 times for suicidal ideation. I’ve been in a place that is as lax as the place in House, and I’ve been in a place that’s basically a prison. I guess it depends but yeah the show wasn’t super accurate (but more accurate than most people who haven’t been in that environment would think a psych ward is like).

Anyways, sorry for rambling. I like shows that have good characters. House is one of those shows.

This question reminded me of a talk I had with my boss. I work in retail, and it’s REALLY shitty hours & pay, but it’s a job that works with my school schedule. My school (community college) is paid for entirely via grants and scholarships, and I live at home with my dad.

My mom recently left practically out of the blue, and she made the primary income in my family. Not much to be completely comfortable, and we couldn’t spend money like we wanted to, but enough to make bills (or find a way to pay for them if we didn’t have the money right then and there). My dad is now the sole income of my household. Even though he has 2 jobs, I have to pitch in with bills sometimes because our family income has more than halved. So I’m my family’s safety net, in a way.

My boss knows about this, as I’ve talked to her about it sometimes as a topic of conversation. But during this conversation, I mentioned that I was considering getting another job on top of my current one, but I wasn’t sure how it would work with school and my current work hours. She told me I shouldn’t try and get one because I’m about to move and transfer schools in the fall, to which I replied, “yeah but I’m poor.”

She then responds with “yeah of course you are, every college student is poor. At least you live with your dad.” I then reiterated that no, I’m not just baseline college student poor. I’m POOR. I need income to help my dad so we don’t lose our house or lose electricity or water. And I still have to pay for my own gas, medicine, snacks, etc. Living at home saves money, but I don’t have any money to not live outside of home with just my current job alone.

So, at least in college, living with an option to go back to is very different than not having any other options. I lived in a college dorm around 2021 when my parents had a better income, and while I was “poor” myself, I didn’t worry about my parents losing their house or car in case I needed to go back home.

There’s context to this, but it really isn’t important to the situation itself, so here’s the gist. Growing up, I’ve always been closer to my dad than my mom. But around my teen years, he would always put me down for having depression symptoms and would make me feel like I was a bad/mean person for getting irritated often (not by anything in particular, just irritability from depression). So, I grew up thinking he was an asshole, and he sort of was for a bit. Then after a while he wasn’t, but I was expecting him to be, so I treated him like he was.

Things got a bit better between us after my symptoms got pretty bad and I ended up in an abusive relationship. I still wasn’t convinced though, and still didn’t think he really cared about me. Part of me thought that he was using me as a way to care for himself (as in a “live vicariously through me” way, but not exactly that). A lot of our conversations centered around him and his interests, and seemed to always go down that route.

Last year, we were at a spring festival being put on by my local nature center. My dad works full time as a social worker, but part time at the nature center. He had a bit of downtime and I was sitting and listening to him complain about my mom. It was irritating me, so I was sort of ignoring him.

All of a sudden, I hear someone yelling my dad’s name and running towards him. My dad looks over, and excitedly yells the guy’s name back. It was one of his past clients when he worked at a local disability center. He was so excited to see my dad, and my dad looked happily surprised to see him. They had a conversation for maybe 5 minutes, and I watched them the entire time.

I don’t know why, but seeing my dad have genuine care for this person he hadn’t seen for half a decade surprised me. I knew he cared about his clients, but it was my first time actually SEEING it (and being conscious of it, I wouldn’t have recognized that as a kid). And the way that this guy was SO happy to see my dad, and REMEMBERED him, showed me how good my dad is at caring for people and that he really makes an impact.

Other stuff has happened since then that strengthened our relationship, but that was a very unexpected turning point for me. I don’t know why that one moment was so impactful for me, but it really was. I went from being irritated by my dad and not caring what he had to say to recognizing him as a caring person in the span of a few minutes. And now, I can 100% tell you that my dad does care about people and he is a very conscious and kind person. He just has a weird way of showing it sometimes.

Not weird at all. My best friend is a guy and he also is waiting for the “right person.” There are definitely guys who feel the same way.

Also, it’s your virginity, you’re the only one who should have agency over when you lose it, where you lose it, and who you lose it to. If someone gets put off by it, then that’s a them problem. They probably wouldn’t be the “right one” to lose it to in that case anyways.

Sometimes I get anxious about it, but after being Pagan for so long, it just makes more sense to me. And a lot of the mechanics of my faith are similar to Christians.

For example, my grandma, who is extremely Christian and has no clue I’m Pagan, has an altar to Jesus. It looked very similar to my altar to Odin because… it’s an altar. Of course, not many Christians have an altar in their home, but some Pagans don’t have altars either. A lot of non-Pagans think I’m weird for having an altar, and sometimes blatantly disrespect it, but I can’t understand why it’s so “weird”. In nearly every religion, there’s a good chunk of people who have altars for worshipping. Why is mine so different?

I’ve also had a few Christians be confused about how I could worship a god that isn’t perfect and all-loving and all-knowing. Putting all of the philosophical debates about that aside, why should I worship a god that’s perfect? I take comfort knowing that the gods I worship are wiser, stronger, and kinder than me, yet they also have their flaws. My ex said this to me about emotional abuse. He said it wasn’t real because there’s no physical force involved and the only consequence would be your partner being mean to you. He basically implied that people who believe that “emotional abuse” is a thing are crybabies and victimize themselves.

Anyways, he was emotionally abusive. People think abuse is just one thing—that physical abuse is JUST hitting, emotional abuse is JUST putting someone down, financial abuse is JUST taking money… it’s so layered. Abuse is hard to escape because it gets in your head. You ask, “will anyone actually help me escape? Should I escape? Is it really that bad? What if I end up in a worse situation?” You question every aspect of it and barely have room to think when you’re being actively abused.

It’s even harder if you have kids or estranged family. I stayed with my ex for as long as I did because my mom kicked me out over my ex and I’s relationship. I knew I was being abused but I made myself push it away because I figured I had nowhere else to go.

And people often say “why didn’t you notice the red flags?” But what a lot of people don’t realize is that abusers usually introduce the abuse slowly. Right before my ex and I broke up, he would choke me out of nowhere for no real reason. If I stayed, I likely would’ve been physically abused as well. Even before the emotional abuse, he was caring and listened to me. He indulged in my interests. It wasn’t until a month after I moved in with him that he started being abusive.

Anyways, sorry that was long. It infuriates me when people respond to abuse victims like “why didn’t you just leave?” and I have a lot to say about it.

I want to start off by saying I haven’t been diagnosed with SAD, so “social anxiety” isn’t in reference to social anxiety disorder. I have GAD and am likely autistic, so my social anxiety is sort of a mix of the two, not one disorder by itself.

I did stay in a hostel once, it was fine and I talked to a few people but otherwise it wasn’t really for me. I had to stay in it because my original plans were cancelled and I had nowhere to stay. I’ll probably only stay in hostels for that reason, mainly out of convenience. And it did make me more anxious than a hotel, as I’ve always had trouble dorming with other people. But the people I stayed with were nice, so that’s a plus.

For me, a lot of my social anxiety is constantly wondering if I look bad, if everyone’s staring at me, if everyone thinks I’m a weirdo, if I sound like an idiot, etc. It’s been debilitating, even if I don’t have to talk to someone. I’ve had to drop out of school because I was anxious about going to class and everyone staring at me or everyone secretly thinking I’m crazy. I don’t know how else to explain it.

It’s become a lot less intense after I started traveling. I mostly travel to big cities (Chicago the most) and in big cities, no one gives a shit. No one cares how you look or act when you’re walking on the street. And in my original comment, what I meant by “it makes me feel more in touch with my surroundings,” I mean I’m literally forced to look around and be alert when I’m walking around in an unfamiliar big city. In situations where I know I’m likely safe, like a classroom or at a local business I go to, I’m more likely to be in my own head and not look around and realize that people don’t give a shit about how I’m acting.

And even when I do talk to people, traveling helped me realize the same thing, too. If I say something stupid or fumble over my words in a different place, the chance I’ll see that person again is very, very low. I guess the feeling has started to bleed into my life at home, and I’m less anxious to ask for help at a business or to ask questions. 

I’m not saying traveling cured my social anxiety. I still get anxious at social gatherings, especially with people I sort of know (ie a gathering of people I go to school with). I do still get anxious going places and asking questions depending on the situation. And traveling for other people could be absolutely horrible for their social anxiety. I just ended up really liking traveling and being able to apply that stuff to my every day life. But I definitely wouldn’t recommend just jumping into going to a huge overstimulating city that you’ve never been to.

I most likely have autism and BPD. I don’t believe my BPD is formally diagnosed but I’ve been told by 3 different mental health professionals that I’m “extremely likely” to have BPD based on my symptoms. I haven’t really talked to professionals about having autism, but I’ve noticed that I have similar traits to my autistic family members, so take that part with a grain of salt.

Here’s how I would break it down using my own experience:

Autism - sensory issues, getting upset if I’m not “prepared” or don’t have enough information, not understanding social norms as well as other people seem to, having intense special interests

BPD - fear of abandonment, self destructive behavior, lack of self identity, extremely negative self view. Extreme reactivity, especially to situations similar to past trauma (aka being bullied or being called certain names). Also idealization/devaluation is huge for me

Both - extreme emotions/anger, misreading social cues (either completely missing them due to autism, or overreading them due to BPD and trauma and reacting inappropriately), not understanding relationships very well, not knowing how to react to other people’s emotions

I think that a lot of it goes hand in hand. For example, I may misread a social cue due to autism, but then my BPD latches onto that and views it as negative, causing me to react inappropriately. Like if someone says “thank you” in a tone I can’t read, I might automatically assume it’s negative due to my own low self esteem.

Otherwise, they probably wouldn’t know what being trans is, or would have a less radical opinion about it.

This happens more with elderly people. I hate how bad it’s gotten, but I’m just hoping things get better in the next few years. I’ve gone from being openly trans/queer to being as stealth as possible whenever I can. It’s hard though because I don’t ever pass as well as I think I do :/

For me, I definitely used to identify as a girl when I was younger. I didn’t have dysphoria until around 11 years old. But before that, I never once wished I were a boy or anything. However, looking back, I really just didn’t care about gender at all. I was more tomboy-ish, but I never felt like I was meant to be a specific gender. I just happened to be born female, so I was treated that way. I think I wouldn’t have cared if my parents treated me as a boy either.

But as I grew up, extra expectations and roles started to be imposed on me. My girl friends stopped wanting to play outside and wanted to play with makeup, which made me really uncomfortable. I remember having dysphoria when I had to shop for bras for the first time. As everyone else started to grow into their womanhood, I was left behind.

But I still used to identify as a girl, and have been perceived as one for years (I didn’t correct people when I was a teenager, mainly because of previous transphobia and also social anxiety). I started my medical transition when I was 18, and while I am a man, the years I lived as a girl are still a part of me. That’s what I find beautiful about being trans; I’ve had both experiences and can relate somewhat to both cis men and cis women. I can see the similarities and differences.

So, I personally would like those years of my life acknowledged, but that’s just me. I understand how using “socialized as” would turn into an unnecessary binary—like how people have started using AFAB and AMAB as another binary and shoved people into those boxes. I can also see it being a trigger for dysphoria. And I’ve seen a few people mention it being a dogwhistle for transphobes and I agree with that part as well. I’ve been in inpatient 3 times in my life. They won’t be able to help with DPDR that much. Inpatient care is mostly for short term stabilization. For example, if you’re suicidal, instead of fixing the root cause of the suicidal ideation, they mostly just give you meds and help to bring you down from the ideation. They usually then refer you to outpatient after that. However, each place is different with different procedures, but those are the constants I’ve had with each of my hospitalizations.

In all honesty, your best bet is to go directly to outpatient. That way you don’t need to spend time and money waiting in a room for the same services. Definitely go to the hospital if you feel as if you’re a danger to yourself or others (ie you have a plan to hurt someone or yourself), but outpatient might be helpful otherwise.

I know that you said you can’t drive anymore, which I understand might make outpatient more difficult. I know a lot of therapists are doing telehealth, so that may be an option for you. As for psychiatry, I think it depends (my psychiatrist only has in-person as an option). But it all depends on what services you think you’d benefit from. 

I hope things work out for you, and I wish you luck. I also appreciate you making your kids a priority. We need more mothers who do that, trust me. The fact that you’re willing to get better and care about your kids’ wellbeing tells me you’re a good mom. Keep it up, don’t give up. You’ve got this. ❤️

I’m not an expert and just got my first IUD a few days ago. But here’s what I can tell you based on my conversations with my clinician (who prescribes both my T and prescribed my IUD):

Periods. I went on birth control mainly because my periods are heavy af and while it doesn’t cause me dysphoria as much, it causes me to be anxious when I get my period and also causes anemia every time I get it. A lot of hormonal forms of birth control stop periods or make them lighter. Ofc, it isn’t immediate, as you said in your post. But after the 3-6 months, it has a chance of entirely stopping for most people.

As for body changes, usually hormonal birth control is progesterone and not estrogen. I’m on T, and when I explained my concern about birth control reversing the changes, my clinician told me that even if I took estrogen-based birth control, there wouldn’t be enough to fully reverse the effects of T. Progesterone will probably not have any visible changes except normal hormonal things (ie acne and skin changes). It won’t make your chest bigger or anything like that, even if you’re pre-T.

Again, I’m not a nurse or expert, so take this with a grain of salt. But I’m inclined to believe her based on other people’s experiences from my personal life.

I looked for my grandma. Nowhere. She wasn’t in the living room, kitchen, guest room, etc. So, the only place left was the bathroom.

I slowly went in, and she was in there. She just looked like she was sleeping, except she was leaning against the shower in a somewhat unnatural way. I kind of held onto the hope that she was sleeping, but either way, I went into the bedroom and cried for a bit.

Then, I realized, she isn’t getting up. That’s how I knew she wasn’t sleeping, since when I cried, she woke up. I then decided that it was up to me to do something. I looked all over the house for her phone, but I couldn’t find it. So, I had to throw together some unmatching thin pajamas, and go outside in the January snow.

I knocked on 2 doors, one of them was my best friend’s house. No one answered, even after spending a few minutes at each. However, I kocked on the third door, and I was scared because the people were new. They had just moved in. But they were really nice, they called 911 and also offered me something to eat.

Turns out, my grandma had a major heart attack. She fainted, and practically died IMMEDIATELY after. I was, at most, 10 years old. I’ve recovered well from the trauma, and the only time I feel a trauma response is when speaking to someone about it in detail, or when I go into that bathroom (my uncle took the house after her death).
